title: Token emit journeys p50-p95-p99 samplebook
content:
Summary:
This note collects an atypical view of end-to-end request timelines — from raw bytes at ingress through tokenization, model kernel execution, and the first-token emit to the streaming socket. Focus is on stage-by-stage p50/p95/p99 splits across sequence length strata, and on signal that is often missed in standard attach-a-trace workflows: tokenizer and framing overhead, serialization/copy costs, and small-kernel switching penalties for quantized variants.

Why this doc exists:
- We keep seeing regressions at the 95/99 boundary that do not correlate with GPU kernel time spikes.
- Hypothesis: client-facing p99s are dominated by host-side prep + tail effects from KV-cache misses + protocol/device-copy tail.
- Need concrete per-stage numbers plus suggested mitigations and experiment plan.

Methodology (sampling & instrumentation):
- Time window: 2025-10-30 -> 2025-11-01 (48h).
- Sampled requests: 12,184 completed generation calls across hosted API fleet for model variants: rwd-3b-fp16, rwd-7b-4bit, rwd-13b-fp16.
- Stratified by max_output_tokens: {short: 1-16, mid: 17-64, long: 65-256}; collected equal sample weight from each stratum by random sampling of traces.
- Instrumentation points (host-side micro-timers): ingress-parse, tokenizer, prompt-embed-lookup, prefill-kernel, kv-cache-lookup, attention-kernel (first_n_tokens and continuation), device-to-host copy (first-token), serialization-to-socket, postprocess-safety, streaming-ack.
- Trace export: sampled traces stored as newline-delimited JSON (light), aggregated to compute stage percentiles.
- Warm vs cold: cold start flagged if pod creation event within prior 60s; KV-warm if last-seen kv-entry hit within window.

Aggregate results (per-stratum p50/p95/p99) — numbers in milliseconds, end-to-first-token (E2F) plus per-stage breakdown:

Short (1-16 tokens) - sample size 4,005
- E2F p50: 42 ms, p95: 118 ms, p99: 243 ms
- Median stage breakdown (p50): tokenizer 6 ms, embed-lookup 3 ms, prefill-kernel 10 ms, kv-cache 1 ms, attention-first-token 12 ms, memcpy-host 4 ms, serialization 3 ms, streaming handshake 3 ms
- p95 dominant contributors: memcpy-host spikes (median 6ms -> p95 68ms), kv-cache miss tail (p95 adds ~20ms), pod-level GC pauses observed in ~2% of traces adding 40-80ms.
- p99: outliers include combined small-protobuf serialization stalls and network congestion to edge node (observed as 80-160ms additional).

Mid (17-64 tokens) - sample size 4,089
- E2F p50: 58 ms, p95: 180 ms, p99: 380 ms
- Median stage breakdown (p50): tokenizer 9 ms, embed-lookup 4 ms, prefill-kernel 15 ms, kv-cache 2 ms, attention-first-token 18 ms, memcpy-host 5 ms, serialization 4 ms, streaming 1 ms
- Observations: attention kernel scales roughly linearly with prefix length; prefill kernel variance increases with mixed-quant encoded tensors.
- p95 drivers: kernel scheduling jitter (NCCL/stream contention) and device-to-host copy queues leading to 120-220ms tails.

Long (65-256 tokens) - sample size 4,090
- E2F p50: 120 ms, p95: 360 ms, p99: 930 ms
- Median stage breakdown (p50): tokenizer 16 ms, embed-lookup 8 ms, prefill-kernel 42 ms, kv-cache 6 ms, attention-first-token 30 ms, memcpy-host 10 ms, serialization 6 ms, streaming 2 ms
- p95/p99: large variance from batching/coalescing windows (some requests batched with older requests causing queuing delays), and from path where prefill triggers fallback to slower quantized kernel due to mixed precision mismatch.

Warm vs Cold analysis (short requests):
- Warm E2F p95: 96 ms. Cold E2F p95: 208 ms.
- Cold traces show 30–80ms extra spent in pod init and JIT/priming steps (rwd-7b-4bit), and KV population penalty (first few tokens include cache fill operations that are charged synchronously).

Notable micro-pathologies we observed (novel findings):
1) Tokenizer I/O burst: for embeddings-heavy prompts (many short tokens), the tokenizer stage sometimes performs repeated normalization loops due to legacy text-framing code; that loop can add 5–12ms and is correlated with certain UTF-8 combos from third-party clients.
2) Protobuf framing stall: small but expensive copies when streaming responses: code path allocates transient buffers that trigger malloc slow paths under memory pressure; empirically responsible for 40–120ms p99 spikes in short requests.
3) KV-key hashing hotspot: concurrent hash table resizing on shared pod-level cache under mixed traffic patterns produced ~30–90ms tails; mutex contention visible in flamegraphs.
4) Kernel switch penalty on hybrid-quant runs: when the runtime detects a queued request whose tensor layout doesn't match the currently bound kernel, it issues a kernel-switch command; this has a fixed ~25ms overhead plus the kernel warm-up variance.

Representative single-trace example (short request, p99 bucket):
- total_e2f: 292 ms
- ingress-parse: 2 ms
- tokenizer: 9 ms (UTF-norm loop x2)
- embed-lookup: 4 ms
- prefill-kernel: 12 ms
- kv-cache-lookup: 1 ms (miss -> sync write 18 ms)
- attention-first-token: 22 ms
- device-to-host copy: 112 ms (blocked behind other copy on host; seen on node gpu-srv-37)
- serialization-to-socket: 6 ms
- streaming-ack-wait: 6 ms
Notes: device-to-host copy here dominates; root cause appears to be pinned-buffer churn and host PCIe DMA scheduling micro-contention.

Actionable mitigations (ranked):
A) Short-term (1–2 sprints):
- Avoid per-request malloc churn in streaming path: reuse frame buffers via a pool (owner: Priya, ticket: RT-3420).
- Add bounded async kv prefetch for likely prefixes to reduce synchronous cache fills (owner: Diego, ticket: RT-3419).
- Introduce host-side prioritized copy queue for first-token copies to reduce head-of-line blocking (owner: Marcus, spike ticket: RT-3435).

B) Medium-term (quarter):
- Kernel binding optimizer: when mixing quantized and fp kernels, schedule similar-layout requests together or maintain two persistent kernel contexts to reduce switch overhead (owner: eng-serving-runtime infra subteam).
- Replace legacy tokenizer normalization loop with streaming normalization that avoids re-checks; add fuzz test for problematic UTF-8 combos.

C) Instrumentation gaps to close:
- Add stack sampling during memcpy-host tails to confirm DMA vs syscall stalls.
- Expose per-request malloc stats in trace export (current traces only include alloc counts).
- Correlate pod-level GC/GC pauses to allocator metrics at process level.

Experiment plan (quick A/B):
- Experiment 1: Buffer pool on streaming path (Priya) — rollout to 10% of short-request traffic, measure p95/p99 E2F delta over 72h.
- Experiment 2: Async KV prefill (Diego) — enable prefetch for top-200 prompt patterns 10% traffic, measure reduction in sync kvWrites and p95.
- Experiment 3: First-token priority copy queue (Marcus) — deploy to dedicated nodes, compare device-to-host copy tail distribution.

Open questions / risks:
- Will buffer pooling increase resident memory beyond acceptable limits? (need memory/pressure sim)
- Async kv prefetch correctness on multi-tenant pods — staleness concerns.
- Kernel-binding changes require scheduler-level work; risk of regressions on throughput.

Immediate next steps (this week):
- Priya: implement and bench buffer pool in dev environment (due 2025-11-07).
- Diego: prototype async kv prefetch stub with metrics (due 2025-11-10).
- Marcus: run host-copy microbench on nodes under load to reproduce 1–200ms tails (due 2025-11-09).
- Product / Solutions: review impact on SLAs for Dedicated customers before rolling kernel-binding changes.

Appendix: notable trace ids (for reproduction) — stored in trace-store, queryable by id:
- trace:ts-20251031-11023-node-gpu-srv-37
- trace:ts-20251031-22195-node-gpu-srv-42
- trace:ts-20251031-04112-node-gpu-srv-09

Footer / context:
This is a working note intended to seed tactical fixes and experiments. It intentionally mixes quantitative percentiles with actionable engineering hypotheses. Expect follow-up with concrete PRs as owners complete the spikes.

End of doc.
